svg.aria-label: Virtual WAN routing intent and policies: the two policy types, the irreversible route table change and its prerequisites, what crosses hubs and what does not, the eligible appliance list and address space limit, and the interactions with hub sizing
svg.title: Routing intent replaces route management rather than adding to it: it cannot coexist with a custom route table, and the change it makes to the default route table is irreversible
svg.text: Two declarations replace the whole route table apparatus — and the swap is one-way
TWO POLICIES, ONE OF EACH PER HUB, ONE NEXT HOP EACH
Internet
Virtual WAN advertises a default 0.0.0.0/0 route to all spokes, gateways and NVAs.
The next hop inspects, then forwards straight out — “direct access”.
Private
ALL branch-to-branch, branch-to-VNet, VNet-to-branch AND inter-hub traffic
through the next hop. With an on-prem or NVA default route this IS forced tunnelling.
Private traffic cannot be subdivided: branch and VNet prefixes are treated as ONE entity.
Cannot be configured at all on a plain hub — it is the control plane for a security appliance that already exists.
THE PRICE OF ADMISSION
Routing intent MANAGES route table associations and propagations for every connection. So a Virtual
WAN with custom route tables or customised policies cannot use it AT ALL. No partial adoption.
Prerequisites
no custom route tables (only noneRouteTable and defaultRouteTable) and no static
routes whose next hop is a VNet connection. Otherwise the option is GREYED OUT.
The change to the defaultRouteTable is IRREVERSIBLE. Removing routing intent sets all connections
to the default label — it does NOT restore what was there. Save your own copy first; nothing will.
The resulting state can differ between the portal and REST, CLI or PowerShell. With a Private policy, connections propagate to noneRouteTable — nowhere.
WHAT CROSSES HUBS, AND WHAT NEVER DOES
The default route does NOT propagate across hubs. Internet egress is strictly LOCAL.
So you cannot build one secured hub and route every other hub’s internet traffic through it. Each hub
needing inspected egress needs its OWN firewall, NVA or SaaS — a per-region licence and appliance.
Same principle as VPN gateways never advertising a default route onward: Azure will not let one propagate past the device that learned it.
Private traffic DOES cross
and in a two-secured-hub setup an inter-hub flow traverses
BOTH firewalls — double inspection, double latency, two processing bills.
Routing intent is the ONLY mechanism for inter-hub inspection, and must be on EVERY hub for symmetry.
WHAT CAN BE THE NEXT HOP, AND HOW MANY SPOKES FIT
Only FOUR named NVAs are eligible:
checkpoint · fortinet-ngfw · fortinet-ngfw-and-sdwan · cisco-tdv-vwan-nva
Specify any other and routing intent CREATION FAILS. Palo Alto Cloud NGFW counts as SaaS.
Unavailable entirely in 21Vianet. In Azure Government, NVA support is limited and SaaS unsupported.
An SD-WAN NVA and a firewall NVA or SaaS cannot share one hub — SD-WAN connectivity is impacted.
The limit is 600 ADDRESS SPACES per hub, not 600 virtual networks:
180 VNets × 3 address spaces each = 540 — already the 90% action threshold.
Was 400, raised to 600, and 600 CANNOT be increased further. Remote hubs’ VNets do not count.
Two failure modes: above 90% ENABLING may fail (loud). On an enabled hub, a newly added address
space may simply NOT BE ROUTABLE (silent). The portal does not surface the count.
TWO INTERACTIONS WITH HUB SIZING
Routing intent BYPASSES the hub router.
The platform programs the data path
directly, router data processing is NOT charged for it, and no extra routing
infrastructure units are needed for forwarding — only for VM count.
A firewall NVA and a SaaS solution share ONE SUBNET
inside a hub address space that
cannot be resized, so running both starves the SaaS solution’s scale-out.
At most ONE SaaS solution per hub.
Encrypted ExpressRoute with routing intent needs an explicit firewall rule between the VPN tunnel endpoints — otherwise the firewall blocks the tunnel it protects.
Per-connection escape from the internet policy: set the propagate-default-route flag false. Per connection, not per subnet.
Static routes can still exist via BGP peering or on the VNet connection, and are applied to the private policy next hop
— but the bypass next hop setting is then ignored.
